cases.answer: The Thai consensus says the work-up of apparent treatment-resistant hypertension should aim to exclude pseudo-resistant hypertension. It lists four requirements: (1) standardized office BP measurement; (2) confirmation of adherence to antihypertensive therapy; (3) exclusion of drug- or substance-induced resistant hypertension; and (4) 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring, using home BP monitoring if ABPM is not available, to exclude the white-coat effect.

cases.answer: Added drug: the Cameroon trial (Djoumessi et al.) added low-dose spironolactone, 25 mg daily, to ongoing therapy in 17 patients with resistant hypertension and type 2 diabetes (9 spironolactone vs 8 on an alternative antihypertensive regimen). The EMPEROR-Preserved resHTN analysis studied empagliflozin vs placebo in HFpEF patients with resistant hypertension. Follow-up: the Cameroon trial lasted four weeks, with visits at 2 and 4 weeks. The EMPEROR-Preserved analysis reported BP out to about Week 172, so it was much longer. I did not find a median follow-up stated in the text I searched. BP change: in Cameroon, office systolic BP fell by 33 mmHg with spironolactone vs 14 mmHg with the alternative regimen (p = 0.024), and diastolic BP fell by 14 vs 5 mmHg (p = 0.006). In EMPEROR-Preserved resHTN, empagliflozin reduced SBP only slightly more than placebo: the mean treatment difference was 2.4 to 3.3 mmHg at Weeks 4-32, and values were similar from Weeks 52-172.

cases.ambiguity: EMPEROR-Preserved follow-up could mean the BP-analysis window (up to Week 172) or the trial's median follow-up, which I did not find in the text. Reported BP change in EMPEROR is a between-arm (empagliflozin vs placebo) difference, whereas Cameroon reports within-arm change for each group.

cases.answer: The Gao et al. CCTA nomogram does not report a ten-year hard-MACE risk. It is a one-year model, with MACE assessed at 1-year follow-up. MACE was mostly soft endpoints, mainly rehospitalization for unstable angina. The only externally validated rate given is the 1-year MACE incidence of 31.60% (91 of 288) in the external validation cohort, about twice the 16.43% in the derivation cohort. The authors note the model is best suited to short-term outcomes and needs validation with longer follow-up and harder outcomes. The derivation cohort size is stated inconsistently: n = 131 in the introduction and n = 280 in the results.
